summary: Argentina lies in southern South America, with territory stretching from the subtropics to Tierra del Fuego near Antarctica, and is known for tango, football, beef and the Pampas grasslands.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 16th century Spain conquered the Río de la Plata basin and founded Buenos Aires twice, in 1536 and 1580; Catholicism arrived with colonization and became the only legal religion of the colony. From the end of the 19th century to the early 20th century, millions of Italian and Spanish immigrants poured in, further consolidating the dominant position of Catholicism; the constitution of 1853 still stipulates that the federal government 'supports' the Roman Catholic Church. In 2013 the Argentine cardinal Bergoglio was elected Pope Francis, the first pope from the Americas.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has grown rapidly in recent decades, concentrated especially in large cities such as Buenos Aires and among the younger generation. The spread of education, urbanization, and disagreements between society and the Church on issues such as the legalization of same-sex marriage in 2010 and of abortion in 2020 have led many people to leave the Church; a 2019 survey found that nearly two tenths of people identified as having no religion.

ranking.name: Evangelical
ranking.description: Evangelicals are mainly Pentecostals; they began to grow after American preachers held large revival meetings in Buenos Aires in the 1950s, and expanded rapidly after the end of the military government and democratization in the 1980s. They are especially active in the poor neighborhoods on the edges of cities and in the northern provinces, attracting believers through community mutual aid and faith healing, and their share has risen to about 15 percent.

ranking.name: Other religions
ranking.description: Other religions include Judaism and Islam. From the end of the 19th century many Eastern European Jewish immigrants came to Argentina, forming the largest Jewish community in Latin America; the 1994 bombing of the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association (AMIA) in Buenos Aires killed 85 people. Muslims are mostly descendants of Syrian and Lebanese immigrants.

religion.background: Before Spanish colonization, the indigenous peoples of Argentina had their own nature and ancestral spirit beliefs; for example, the belief in the earth mother Pachamama in the northwestern Andes is still alive today. From the 16th century Catholicism expanded with Spanish colonization and Jesuit missions; in the 17th and 18th centuries the Jesuits established mission villages in the Guaraní region of the northeast, until they were expelled by the Spanish king in 1767. The large-scale European immigration of the late 19th century brought many Catholics and also minority religions such as Judaism and Protestantism. Since the late 20th century, both Evangelicals and the non-religious have been increasing, and the Catholic share has gradually declined.

language.official: Spanish is the de facto official language.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish arrived with Spanish colonization in the 16th century. Argentine Spanish is called 'Rioplatense Spanish': it uses 'vos' instead of 'tú', pronounces 'll' and 'y' like 'sh', and, because of the mass arrival of Italian immigrants at the end of the 19th century, carries a strong Italian intonation and vocabulary (such as the Buenos Aires slang lunfardo). Because the indigenous population dropped sharply during colonization and the 19th-century 'Conquest of the Desert' campaigns, Spanish became almost everyone's mother tongue.

ranking.name: Guaraní
ranking.description: Guaraní is spoken mainly in the northeastern provinces bordering Paraguay, such as Corrientes and Misiones; the Jesuit mission villages of the 17th and 18th centuries evangelized in Guaraní, which allowed it to survive in this area. In 2004 Corrientes Province made Guaraní a provincial official language, and in recent years many Paraguayan immigrants have also used it in Buenos Aires.

ranking.name: Quechua
ranking.description: Quechua is the language of the Inca Empire; in the 15th century Inca power expanded into northwestern Argentina, and in the colonial period Spanish missionaries also preached in Quechua. Today it is used mainly in the northwestern regions such as Santiago del Estero and Jujuy provinces, and there are also speakers brought by Bolivian immigrants.

language.history: Before the Spanish arrived, many indigenous languages such as Quechua, Guaraní and Mapudungun were spoken in Argentina. After colonization in the 16th century Spanish became the language of administration and the Church, and after independence in 1816 it became the national language. Between 1870 and 1930 about six million European immigrants poured in, the Italians being the most numerous, deeply influencing the intonation and slang of Argentine Spanish. In the early 20th century the government assimilated the children of immigrants through compulsory Spanish-language education, while indigenous languages continued to shrink, and only in recent years have bilingual education programs been used to preserve them.

ranking.name: Asado
ranking.description: Beef short ribs, sausages, blood sausage and offal are slowly grilled over charcoal or wood, seasoned only with coarse salt, and eaten with chimichurri sauce.
ranking.history: Asado originated with the gauchos of the Pampas in the 18th and 19th centuries, who herded feral cattle and ate beef roasted over fires in the open. In the late 19th century refrigerated ships and railways made Argentina a major beef exporter, and beef also became cheap and common domestically. Today the Sunday family asado is an important social ritual; the person who tends the fire is called the 'asador', and the guests applaud him in appreciation.

ranking.name: Empanada
ranking.description: A half-moon pastry in which dough is wrapped around fillings such as ground beef, onion, olives and boiled egg and then baked or fried; the flavor differs from province to province.
ranking.history: The method of making empanadas can be traced to Galicia in Spain and to even earlier Arab pies, and it came to South America with Spanish colonizers in the 16th century. The provinces of Argentina developed different styles; for example, the versions of Tucumán and Salta in the northwest are famous for hand-cut beef, and Famaillá in Tucumán Province also holds a national empanada festival every year. It is a common food at festivals, gatherings and national holidays (25 May and 9 July).

ranking.name: Milanesa
ranking.description: Thin slices of beef are coated in egg and breadcrumbs and then fried or baked, and often served with mashed potatoes or fries, or made into the Neapolitan style with tomato sauce and cheese.
ranking.history: Milanesa derives from the fried veal cutlet of Milan in Italy (cotoletta alla milanese), and came to Argentina with the large wave of Italian immigrants from the end of the 19th century to the early 20th century, using the cheap local beef instead. The famous 'milanesa a la napolitana' is said to have been created in the 1940s by a Buenos Aires restaurant called 'Nápoli' and has nothing to do with the city of Naples itself. Today it is one of the most common everyday dishes in Argentine households.

ranking.name: Dulce de Leche
ranking.description: Milk and sugar are cooked slowly over low heat for a long time until the sugar and proteins caramelize into a thick, caramel-colored sweet sauce that can be spread on bread or used as a dessert filling.
ranking.history: Similar milk caramels exist throughout Latin America, and in Argentina a legend circulates that in 1829, during a meeting between the political rivals Rosas and Lavalle, a maid forgot the sweetened milk on the stove and it accidentally became dulce de leche, but this story has no reliable historical source. After the 19th century it became popular in Argentina, used in the filling of alfajor sandwich cookies, in crêpes and in ice cream. Argentines regard it as a national symbol and have sought to have it listed as cultural heritage.

ranking.name: Locro
ranking.description: A thick stew cooked for a long time from white corn, beans and pumpkin with beef, pork and sausage; the flavor is rich and hearty, and it is suited to eating in winter.
ranking.history: Locro derives from the corn and pumpkin stews of the Andean indigenous peoples, already eaten before the Inca era, and after colonization the pork and sausage brought by the Spanish were added. During the independence wars of the 19th century it became a patriotic symbol, and today Argentines traditionally eat locro on 25 May, the anniversary of the May Revolution (1810), and on 9 July, Independence Day (1816). It is also a home dish of the northern provinces in winter.
